questions.question_text: South Dakota water rights follow which legal doctrine?
distractors: Riparian rights
Correlative rights
Reasonable use doctrine
questions.explanation: South Dakota allocates water by prior appropriation — the earliest priority date holds the better right (SDCL 46-1-3). Domestic use is the one exception: it is the highest use and comes ahead of all appropriative rights.

questions.question_text: A buyer is purchasing farmland in western South Dakota. Why is it important to verify the mineral rights status?
questions.correct_answer: Mineral rights may be severed from surface rights
distractors: Mineral rights always transfer with the land
Only the state government may own mineral rights
Mineral rights must be re-recorded every five years
questions.explanation: Mineral rights can be severed from the surface, so a seller may own the land but not what lies beneath it — verify the record before closing. A severed interest unused for 23 years can also be deemed abandoned and vest in the surface owner (SDCL 43-30A-2).

questions.question_text: In 2025, South Dakota passed significant legislation regarding eminent domain. What was prohibited?
questions.correct_answer: Eminent domain for CO2 pipeline projects
distractors: All private use of eminent domain power
Eminent domain for highway construction
Condemnation of any agricultural properties
questions.explanation: House Bill 1052, signed in March 2025, bars the use of eminent domain for any pipeline carrying carbon oxide. Landowners can no longer be forced to grant CO2 pipeline easements through condemnation, though voluntary easements remain available.

questions.question_text: A rural SD property relies on well water. What concern should the buyer's agent raise?
questions.correct_answer: Potential well water quality and contamination issues
distractors: Wells are illegal on residential properties
Municipal water must be connected within 1 year
The seller must drill a new well before closing
questions.explanation: Rural SD properties often rely on well water, and buyers should be concerned about water quality issues including agricultural chemical contamination. Agents should advise buyers to have well water tested as part of their due diligence.

questions.question_text: Under prior appropriation, who has the superior right to use water from a shared source in South Dakota?
questions.correct_answer: The appropriator with the earliest priority date
distractors: The person whose property is closest to the source
The person with the largest parcel of land
All adjacent property owners have equal rights
questions.explanation: Priority runs from the date the appropriation was applied for — first in time, first in right (SDCL 46-1-3). Domestic use outranks every appropriative right regardless of priority date and generally needs no permit.

questions.question_text: How long must a severed mineral interest go unused before South Dakota deems it abandoned?
distractors: 20 years
30 years
It never lapses
questions.explanation: A severed mineral interest that goes unused for 23 years or more is deemed abandoned, and title vests in the owner of the surface estate (SDCL 43-30A-2). Twenty years is the common period in other states, but South Dakota's runs longer.

questions.question_text: A surface owner wants to take title to a mineral interest that has lapsed for nonuse. What notice must the surface owner give?
questions.correct_answer: Publish notice once a week for three weeks
distractors: Post notice at the courthouse for thirty days
Publish notice once in a statewide newspaper
Record an affidavit of nonuse and wait one year
questions.explanation: The surface owner must publish notice of the lapse once each week for three weeks in the county's official newspaper (SDCL 43-30A-6). A certified copy must also be mailed to the record mineral owner within ten days after the final publication.

questions.question_text: A surface owner publishes notice that a severed mineral interest has lapsed. How can the mineral owner defeat the claim?
questions.correct_answer: Record a statement of claim within 60 days of publication
distractors: File suit to quiet title within one year of the published notice
Pay the surface owner's publication and recording costs
Nothing — the lapse is final once the notice has run
questions.explanation: Recording a statement of claim within 60 days after the notice of lapse finishes publishing preserves the mineral interest, even if the owner missed the earlier deadline (SDCL 43-30A-5). Almost any use of the interest during the 23 years also defeats abandonment.

questions.question_text: A carbon oxide pipeline developer cannot reach terms with a South Dakota landowner. May it condemn the right-of-way?
questions.correct_answer: No — but the company may still negotiate a voluntary easement
distractors: Yes — condemnation is available once a siting permit is issued
No — and a voluntary easement would be barred for the same reason
Yes — provided the pipeline is operated as a common carrier
questions.explanation: Eminent domain may not be used to acquire right-of-way for a carbon oxide pipeline, even by a common carrier (SDCL 49-7-13.1, added by 2025's HB 1052). The developer's only route is an easement the landowner agrees to sign.

questions.question_text: South Dakota's HJR 5001 would have written eminent domain limits into the state constitution. How did the measure end?
questions.correct_answer: The Senate defeated it, keeping it off the ballot
distractors: Voters ratified it at the 2026 general election
The governor vetoed it after both chambers passed
The Senate amended it into a statute and passed it
questions.explanation: Amending the South Dakota Constitution requires both chambers to adopt a joint resolution before the question can reach the voters. HJR 5001 cleared the House in January 2026 but failed in the Senate that March, so South Dakota's eminent domain limits remain statutory.
